english: to depart, to set off (to go somewhere) to leave (on a trip)
note: "Berangkat" refers to setting off or departing for a destination; commonly confused with "pergi" (to go) — "berangkat" emphasizes the moment of leaving, often used for trips, school, or work; related: "keberangkatan" (departure).

sentences.text: Saya berangkat ke sekolah pukul tujuh.
sentences.en: I leave for school at seven o'clock.

sentences.text: Kami berangkat ke Bali besok pagi.
sentences.en: We depart for Bali tomorrow morning.

sentences.text: Bus itu berangkat dari terminal sekarang.
sentences.en: The bus is departing from the terminal now.

note: "Berkunjung (ke)" means to visit a place (not a person); use "mengunjungi" for visiting people; common in polite or written speech.

sentences.text: Kami berkunjung ke pura hari ini.
sentences.en: We are visiting a temple today.

sentences.text: Dia berkunjung ke pasar setiap minggu.
sentences.en: She visits the market every week.

sentences.text: Saya ingin berkunjung ke Bali.
sentences.en: I want to visit Bali.

note: "Kurang" means "to" or "before" when telling the time, e.g. "kurang lima" = "five to"; often confused with "kurang" meaning "less/not enough".

sentences.text: Sekarang jam tiga kurang sepuluh menit.
sentences.en: It is now ten to three.

sentences.text: Bus datang jam delapan kurang lima.
sentences.en: The bus arrives at five to eight.

sentences.text: Kelas mulai jam sembilan kurang seperempat.
sentences.en: Class starts at a quarter to nine.

english: past (when telling the time),to go past
note: "Lewat" means 'past' in time expressions (e.g., jam tiga lewat lima = five past three) and also 'to pass/go past' a place; don't confuse with "melewati" which is the formal verb form.

sentences.text: Sekarang jam dua lewat sepuluh menit.
sentences.en: It is now ten past two.

sentences.text: Bus ini lewat pasar setiap pagi.
sentences.en: This bus goes past the market every morning.

sentences.text: Dia lewat rumah saya tadi.
sentences.en: He passed by my house just now.

note: 'Makan pagi' is the everyday informal term for breakfast; 'sarapan' is a common synonym you will also hear often.

sentences.text: Saya makan pagi di rumah setiap hari.
sentences.en: I have breakfast at home every day.

sentences.text: Kami makan pagi bersama di warung.
sentences.en: We have breakfast together at the warung.

sentences.text: Dia belum makan pagi pagi ini.
sentences.en: She has not had breakfast yet this morning.

note: "Makan siang" literally means "eat midday"; use it for lunch around noon, distinct from "makan pagi" (breakfast) and "makan malam" (dinner).

sentences.text: Saya makan siang di warung setiap hari.
sentences.en: I have lunch at the food stall every day.

sentences.text: Kami makan siang bersama di kantin.
sentences.en: We have lunch together in the canteen.

sentences.text: Dia belum makan siang hari ini.
sentences.en: She has not had lunch yet today.

note: "Makan malam" literally means "eat night" and refers to dinner; similar forms are "makan pagi" (breakfast) and "makan siang" (lunch).

sentences.text: Kami makan malam bersama keluarga setiap hari.
sentences.en: We have dinner together with family every day.

sentences.text: Saya ingin makan malam di restoran ini.
sentences.en: I want to have dinner at this restaurant.

sentences.text: Dia sudah makan malam tadi malam.
sentences.en: She already had dinner last night.

note: "Perusahaan" means a formal company or business enterprise; more formal than "toko" (shop) or "usaha" (small business/effort).

sentences.text: Ayah saya bekerja di perusahaan besar.
sentences.en: My father works at a big company.

sentences.text: Perusahaan itu menjual air minum.
sentences.en: That company sells drinking water.

sentences.text: Dia ingin bekerja di perusahaan terkenal.
sentences.en: She wants to work at a famous company.

english: o'clock[a marker word used to express the time of day in hours and minutes]
note: "Pukul" is the formal/neutral word for telling time in hours; it is interchangeable with "jam" in many contexts but sounds slightly more formal, and is never used to mean the physical object clock.

sentences.text: Kelas dimulai pukul delapan pagi.
sentences.en: Class starts at eight o'clock in the morning.

sentences.text: Kami makan siang pukul dua belas.
sentences.en: We have lunch at twelve o'clock.

sentences.text: Toko itu tutup pukul sembilan malam.
sentences.en: That shop closes at nine o'clock at night.

english: until (a certain time) as far as (a certain place)
note: "Sampai" is everyday informal/neutral Indonesian for both time ("until") and place ("as far as / to"); very common in spoken Balinese/Indonesian life, often confused with "ke" (simple direction) — use "sampai" when emphasizing the endpoint.

sentences.text: Saya belajar sampai jam sepuluh malam.
sentences.en: I study until ten o'clock at night.

sentences.text: Bus ini pergi sampai pantai Kuta.
sentences.en: This bus goes as far as Kuta beach.

sentences.text: Toko itu buka sampai sore.
sentences.en: That shop is open until the afternoon.

note: 'Sarapan' means both 'breakfast' (noun) and 'to have breakfast' (verb); commonly confused with 'makan pagi' which means the same thing but is slightly more formal.

sentences.text: Saya sarapan nasi goreng setiap pagi.
sentences.en: I have breakfast with fried rice every morning.

sentences.text: Ayo kita sarapan di warung itu!
sentences.en: Let's have breakfast at that small restaurant!

sentences.text: Dia belum sarapan hari ini.
sentences.en: She has not had breakfast today.

note: "Seperempat" means "a quarter" (1/4); commonly used for time (seperempat jam = quarter hour) and fractions of food or money; related: "setengah" (half), "sepertiga" (one third).

sentences.text: Saya makan seperempat semangka di pantai.
sentences.en: I eat a quarter of a watermelon at the beach.

sentences.text: Dia datang seperempat jam yang lalu.
sentences.en: She arrived a quarter of an hour ago.

sentences.text: Berikan aku seperempat kue itu.
sentences.en: Give me a quarter of that cake.

note: "Setengah" means "half" and is used for fractions, time (setengah tiga = 2:30), and quantities; don't confuse with "separuh" which is a near-synonym but less common in daily speech.

sentences.text: Saya minum setengah gelas air putih.
sentences.en: I drink half a glass of water.

sentences.text: Dia makan setengah porsi nasi goreng.
sentences.en: She eats half a portion of fried rice.

sentences.text: Sekarang jam setengah delapan pagi.
sentences.en: It is now seven-thirty in the morning.

english: at midnight, in the middle of the night
note: 'Tengah malam' literally means 'middle of the night'; used in everyday speech for midnight or very late at night, similar to 'jam dua belas malam'.

sentences.text: Dia pulang ke rumah tengah malam.
sentences.en: He went home in the middle of the night.

sentences.text: Saya lapar tengah malam.
sentences.en: I am hungry at midnight.

sentences.text: Anjing itu menggonggong tengah malam.
sentences.en: The dog barked in the middle of the night.

note: 'Tertawa' means 'to laugh'; it is a standard/neutral word — related words include 'senyum' (smile) and 'tawa' (laughter/noun form).

sentences.text: Anak-anak tertawa di taman setiap hari.
sentences.en: The children laugh in the park every day.

sentences.text: Kami tertawa bersama saat makan malam.
sentences.en: We laugh together during dinner.

sentences.text: Dia tertawa karena cerita itu lucu.
sentences.en: She laughs because the story is funny.

note: "Apaan" is informal/slang for "apa" (what), often expressing surprise or mild annoyance; avoid in formal speech; related to "apa ini" (what is this).

sentences.text: Apaan ini, kok aneh banget?
sentences.en: What is this, it's so weird?

sentences.text: Kamu makan apaan tadi?
sentences.en: What kind of thing did you eat just now?

sentences.text: Apaan sih, itu bukan makananku!
sentences.en: What the heck, that's not my food!

note: 'Banget' is informal/slang for 'very' or 'really'; placed after the adjective (e.g. 'enak banget'), common in everyday speech; formal equivalent is 'sekali'.

sentences.text: Makanan ini enak banget!
sentences.en: This food is really delicious!

sentences.text: Cuacanya panas banget hari ini.
sentences.en: The weather is very hot today.

sentences.text: Saya capek banget setelah jalan jauh.
sentences.en: I am really tired after walking far.

english: fixed up, put right, all okay, resolved
note: 'Beres' is informal/colloquial, used to mean everything is settled or done; similar to 'sudah selesai' but more casual; related: 'beres-beres' means to tidy up.

sentences.text: Kamar saya sudah beres sekarang.
sentences.en: My room is all tidied up now.

sentences.text: Masalah itu sudah beres, terima kasih.
sentences.en: That problem is resolved now, thank you.

sentences.text: Apakah semuanya sudah beres?
sentences.en: Is everything all okay?

note: 'berlari' is the standard verb 'to run'; related words include 'lari' (run/noun) and 'berlari-lari' (to run around/leisurely); used in everyday and formal contexts.

sentences.text: Anak itu berlari di pantai setiap pagi.
sentences.en: That child runs on the beach every morning.

sentences.text: Saya berlari ke sekolah karena terlambat.
sentences.en: I run to school because I am late.

sentences.text: Mereka berlari bersama di taman.
sentences.en: They run together in the park.

note: 'Doyan' is informal/slang for liking food or activities; avoid in formal writing; similar to 'suka' but more colloquial and often implies craving or being fond of eating something.

sentences.text: Saya doyan makan nasi goreng setiap pagi.
sentences.en: I really like eating fried rice every morning.

sentences.text: Anak itu doyan sekali minum es teh.
sentences.en: That child really loves drinking iced tea.

sentences.text: Kamu doyan buah mangga tidak?
sentences.en: Do you like mangoes?

english: to attend a lecture, to go to a lecture
note: "Ikut" means to join/follow/attend; "ikut kuliah" is a natural colloquial way to say attending a lecture, more casual than "menghadiri kuliah"; also related: "ikut kelas" (attend class).

sentences.text: Hari ini saya ikut kuliah di kampus.
sentences.en: Today I attend a lecture at the campus.

sentences.text: Dia tidak ikut kuliah kemarin.
sentences.en: She did not attend the lecture yesterday.

sentences.text: Besok kamu ikut kuliah bersama kami?
sentences.en: Are you going to the lecture with us tomorrow?

note: "Jam berapa?" means "what time?" and is used to ask the time; pair it with "sekarang" (now) for "what time is it now?"

sentences.text: Jam berapa kita berangkat ke pantai?
sentences.en: What time do we leave for the beach?

sentences.text: Maaf, jam berapa warung ini buka?
sentences.en: Excuse me, what time does this food stall open?

sentences.text: Jam berapa kamu makan malam?
sentences.en: What time do you have dinner?

english: (slangy) if as for (me/him/that etc.) as far as ... is concerned (informal)
note: "Kalo" is an informal/slang contraction of "kalau" (if / as for); very common in casual speech but avoid in formal writing.

sentences.text: Kalo lapar, kita makan di warung.
sentences.en: If (you're) hungry, let's eat at the food stall.

sentences.text: Kalo aku, suka nasi goreng.
sentences.en: As for me, I like fried rice.

sentences.text: Kalo hujan, aku di rumah.
sentences.en: If it rains, I stay at home.

note: Informal spoken form of 'bertemu' (to meet) and 'menemukan' (to find); very common in everyday speech but avoid in formal writing.

sentences.text: Saya ketemu teman lama di pasar.
sentences.en: I met an old friend at the market.

sentences.text: Dia ketemu dompetnya di kursi.
sentences.en: She found her wallet on the chair.

sentences.text: Kita ketemu besok di kafe, ya?
sentences.en: We'll meet tomorrow at the café, okay?

english: a field, a (sports) ground, an open space (especially for recreation)
note: "Lapangan" is neutral/everyday register; commonly used for sports fields and open plazas; related words: "ladang" (farm field), "lapangan terbang" (airport).

sentences.text: Anak-anak bermain bola di lapangan.
sentences.en: The children are playing football on the field.

sentences.text: Lapangan itu sangat luas dan hijau.
sentences.en: The field is very wide and green.

sentences.text: Kami berlari di lapangan setiap pagi.
sentences.en: We run on the field every morning.

note: "Lebih suka" means to prefer or like something better; use it before a noun or verb, e.g. "lebih suka makan" (prefer to eat); related: "suka" (to like).

sentences.text: Saya lebih suka nasi daripada roti.
sentences.en: I prefer rice over bread.

sentences.text: Dia lebih suka minum teh setiap pagi.
sentences.en: She prefers to drink tea every morning.

sentences.text: Kami lebih suka pantai daripada gunung.
sentences.en: We prefer the beach over the mountain.

note: 'Lumayan' is casual/colloquial, used to say something is 'not bad' or 'pretty good'; avoid confusing it with 'cukup' (enough/sufficient).

sentences.text: Makanan di sini lumayan enak.
sentences.en: The food here is pretty good.

sentences.text: Harganya lumayan murah untuk wisatawan.
sentences.en: The price is quite cheap for tourists.

sentences.text: Cuacanya lumayan panas hari ini.
sentences.en: The weather is quite hot today.

note: "Nanti siang" means 'this afternoon' and is used in the morning when referring to later that same day; don't confuse with "tadi siang" (earlier this afternoon) or "siang ini" (a more formal equivalent).

sentences.text: Kita makan soto nanti siang, ya?
sentences.en: We'll eat soto this afternoon, okay?

sentences.text: Nanti siang ada hujan di Bali.
sentences.en: This afternoon there will be rain in Bali.

sentences.text: Saya ke pasar nanti siang.
sentences.en: I'm going to the market this afternoon.

english: late this afternoon (spoken earlier in the day)
note: "Nanti sore" means "later this afternoon" and is used when speaking earlier in the day; "nanti" alone means "later" and "sore" means "afternoon/evening" (roughly 3–6 PM).

sentences.text: Kita pergi ke pantai nanti sore.
sentences.en: We are going to the beach later this afternoon.

sentences.text: Dia akan datang nanti sore.
sentences.en: He/She will come later this afternoon.

sentences.text: Saya makan nasi goreng nanti sore.
sentences.en: I will eat fried rice later this afternoon.

note: Used to say 'tonight' when speaking earlier in the day; 'malam ini' is also common but 'nanti malam' emphasizes the future sense.

sentences.text: Kita makan bersama nanti malam, ya?
sentences.en: We eat together tonight, okay?

sentences.text: Nanti malam ada pertunjukan di pantai.
sentences.en: Tonight there is a show at the beach.

sentences.text: Saya tidur awal nanti malam.
sentences.en: I will sleep early tonight.

note: "Pake" is an informal/colloquial form of "pakai" (to use/with/by); very common in spoken Indonesian but avoid in formal writing.

sentences.text: Saya pergi ke pasar pake motor.
sentences.en: I go to the market by motorbike.

sentences.text: Dia ke sekolah pake sepeda.
sentences.en: She goes to school by bicycle.

sentences.text: Kamu mau ke pantai pake apa?
sentences.en: How do you want to get to the beach?

english: to come home, to go home
note: 'Pulang' means to go/come home; use 'pulang ke rumah' for emphasis; often confused with 'pergi' (to go out).

sentences.text: Saya pulang ke rumah setelah bekerja.
sentences.en: I go home after working.

sentences.text: Dia pulang dari sekolah sore ini.
sentences.en: She comes home from school this afternoon.

sentences.text: Kami pulang naik sepeda motor bersama.
sentences.en: We go home together by motorbike.

english: [a slangy particle that adds emphasis and colour to a question]
note: "Sih" is a casual spoken particle used to soften or add mild emphasis to questions and statements; avoid it in formal writing.

sentences.text: Kamu mau makan apa sih malam ini?
sentences.en: So what do you want to eat tonight?

sentences.text: Di mana sih warung nasi itu?
sentences.en: Where on earth is that rice stall?

sentences.text: Kenapa sih kamu tidak datang kemarin?
sentences.en: Why didn't you come yesterday, anyway?

note: "Tentu saja" means "of course" and is polite and natural in everyday speech; similar to "pastinya" but slightly more formal.

sentences.text: Tentu saja saya mau makan nasi goreng.
sentences.en: Of course I want to eat fried rice.

sentences.text: Apakah kamu suka pantai? Tentu saja!
sentences.en: Do you like the beach? Of course!

sentences.text: Tentu saja dia bisa berbicara bahasa Indonesia.
sentences.en: Of course she can speak Indonesian.

note: 'Yuk' is informal/casual, used to invite someone to do something together; similar to 'ayo' but softer and more colloquial.

sentences.text: Yuk, kita makan siang bersama!
sentences.en: C'mon, let's have lunch together!

sentences.text: Yuk pergi ke pantai sekarang.
sentences.en: Let's go to the beach now.

sentences.text: Yuk, kita beli es krim!
sentences.en: C'mon, let's buy ice cream!

note: 'Hari' means 'day' and is used in common phrases like 'hari ini' (today), 'hari ini' vs 'sehari' (one whole day); don't confuse with 'matahari' (sun).

sentences.text: Hari ini saya pergi ke pantai.
sentences.en: Today I am going to the beach.

sentences.text: Setiap hari dia minum kopi pagi.
sentences.en: Every day he drinks morning coffee.

sentences.text: Besok adalah hari libur nasional.
sentences.en: Tomorrow is a national holiday.

english: sometimes, occasionally, from time to time
note: 'Kadang-kadang' is neutral, everyday Indonesian for 'sometimes'; related words include 'sesekali' (once in a while) and 'terkadang' (sometimes, slightly more formal).

sentences.text: Saya kadang-kadang makan nasi goreng di sini.
sentences.en: I sometimes eat fried rice here.

sentences.text: Dia kadang-kadang pergi ke pantai.
sentences.en: He/She sometimes goes to the beach.

sentences.text: Kami kadang-kadang naik sepeda ke pasar.
sentences.en: We sometimes ride a bicycle to the market.

note: 'Musik' is a neutral everyday word for music; used in both formal and informal speech; related words: 'lagu' (song), 'penyanyi' (singer), 'band' (band).

sentences.text: Saya suka mendengarkan musik setiap hari.
sentences.en: I like listening to music every day.

sentences.text: Musik ini sangat enak didengar.
sentences.en: This music sounds very pleasant.

sentences.text: Di Bali, musik tradisional sangat terkenal.
sentences.en: In Bali, traditional music is very famous.

note: "Pada pagi hari" means "in the morning(s)" and is slightly more formal than "pagi-pagi"; often used to describe regular morning routines.

sentences.text: Saya minum kopi pada pagi hari.
sentences.en: I drink coffee in the morning.

sentences.text: Pada pagi hari, dia pergi ke pasar.
sentences.en: In the morning, she goes to the market.

sentences.text: Kami berolahraga pada pagi hari.
sentences.en: We exercise in the morning.

note: 'Pada siang hari' means 'in the afternoon/daytime' (around noon to 3 PM); often confused with 'sore hari' (late afternoon/evening); 'pada' adds a formal time marker.

sentences.text: Saya makan siang pada siang hari.
sentences.en: I eat lunch in the afternoon.

sentences.text: Cuaca sangat panas pada siang hari.
sentences.en: The weather is very hot in the afternoon.

sentences.text: Toko itu tutup pada siang hari.
sentences.en: That shop is closed in the afternoon.

note: "Pada sore hari" means "in the late afternoon" and is a fixed time phrase; beginners often confuse "sore" (late afternoon, ~3–6 pm) with "malam" (evening/night) or "siang" (midday).

sentences.text: Kami minum teh pada sore hari.
sentences.en: We drink tea in the late afternoon.

sentences.text: Dia bermain bola pada sore hari.
sentences.en: He plays football in the late afternoon.

sentences.text: Toko itu tutup pada sore hari.
sentences.en: That shop closes in the late afternoon.

note: 'Pada malam hari' means 'at night'; more formal than 'malam ini' (tonight); often used to describe nightly routines or general nighttime events.

sentences.text: Saya tidur pada malam hari.
sentences.en: I sleep at night.

sentences.text: Bintang terlihat pada malam hari.
sentences.en: Stars are visible at night.

sentences.text: Kami makan bersama pada malam hari.
sentences.en: We eat together at night.

note: 'Salah' means 'wrong' or 'to be wrong'; also used in 'salah satu' (one of); don't confuse with 'tidak benar' which is more formal.

sentences.text: Jawaban kamu salah, coba lagi.
sentences.en: Your answer is wrong, try again.

sentences.text: Maaf, saya salah jalan tadi.
sentences.en: Sorry, I took the wrong road just now.

sentences.text: Itu bukan salah kamu.
sentences.en: That is not your fault.

note: 'Tenis' is a direct loanword for tennis; often paired with 'bermain tenis' (to play tennis) or 'lapangan tenis' (tennis court).

sentences.text: Saya suka bermain tenis setiap minggu.
sentences.en: I like to play tennis every week.

sentences.text: Lapangan tenis di sini sangat bagus.
sentences.en: The tennis court here is very nice.

sentences.text: Dia beli raket tenis baru kemarin.
sentences.en: He/She bought a new tennis racket yesterday.

english: a television/radio program, something you plan to do
note: "Acara" means both a TV/radio program and a planned event or activity; very common in everyday speech.

sentences.text: Acara televisi ini sangat menarik.
sentences.en: This television program is very interesting.

sentences.text: Apa acara kamu malam ini?
sentences.en: What are your plans tonight?

sentences.text: Saya suka acara memasak di TV.
sentences.en: I like the cooking program on TV.

note: 'Apalagi' means 'especially/particularly/all the more so'; often used to strengthen a statement, similar to 'moreover'; don't confuse with 'terutama' which is a closer synonym.

sentences.text: Saya suka nasi goreng, apalagi dengan telur.
sentences.en: I like fried rice, especially with egg.

sentences.text: Hari ini panas, apalagi di pantai.
sentences.en: Today is hot, especially at the beach.

sentences.text: Dia lelah, apalagi setelah kerja lama.
sentences.en: He is tired, especially after working long.

english: an apartment, a flat, a unit
note: "Apartemen" is a loanword from English; used for modern high-rise flats, while "rumah" means a house — don't mix them up.

sentences.text: Saya tinggal di apartemen yang baru.
sentences.en: I live in a new apartment.

sentences.text: Apartemen itu dekat dengan pantai.
sentences.en: That apartment is close to the beach.

sentences.text: Dia menyewa apartemen di Bali.
sentences.en: She rents an apartment in Bali.

note: 'Berenang' is an informal, everyday verb for swimming; often paired with 'pergi' (to go) or used alone; related: 'kolam renang' (swimming pool), 'renang' (swimming as a noun/sport).

sentences.text: Saya suka berenang di pantai setiap pagi.
sentences.en: I like to swim at the beach every morning.

sentences.text: Anak-anak berenang di kolam renang hari ini.
sentences.en: The children are swimming in the pool today.

sentences.text: Dia ingin berenang bersama teman-temannya.
sentences.en: She wants to go swimming with her friends.

english: to rest, to take a rest, to take a break
note: 'Beristirahat' is a formal/neutral verb for resting; in casual speech Indonesians often say 'istirahat' alone; related: 'tidur' (to sleep), 'santai' (to relax).

sentences.text: Saya perlu beristirahat setelah bekerja keras.
sentences.en: I need to rest after working hard.

sentences.text: Anak-anak beristirahat di bawah pohon besar.
sentences.en: The children are resting under the big tree.

sentences.text: Mari kita beristirahat sebentar di sini.
sentences.en: Let's take a short break here.

note: Formal/religious term for prayer or worship, often used in Hindu-Balinese and Islamic contexts; more formal than 'berdoa' (to pray).

sentences.text: Ibu bersembahyang di pura setiap pagi.
sentences.en: Mother worships at the temple every morning.

sentences.text: Kami bersembahyang bersama keluarga hari ini.
sentences.en: We do our prayers together with family today.

english: to do gymnastics, to do aerobics, to work out
note: "Bersenam" is a common informal word for exercising or doing aerobics; often interchangeable with "berolahraga" but more specific to gym-style or aerobic exercise.

sentences.text: Saya bersenam setiap pagi di rumah.
sentences.en: I work out every morning at home.

sentences.text: Ibu suka bersenam bersama teman-temannya.
sentences.en: Mom likes to do aerobics with her friends.

sentences.text: Kami bersenam di taman setiap hari.
sentences.en: We work out in the park every day.

note: 'Cuma' means 'just/only' and is informal/colloquial; in formal writing use 'hanya' instead; commonly used in everyday speech across Indonesia.

sentences.text: Saya cuma mau minum air putih.
sentences.en: I just want to drink plain water.

sentences.text: Harga ini cuma dua puluh ribu.
sentences.en: This price is only twenty thousand.

sentences.text: Dia cuma punya satu baju baru.
sentences.en: She only has one new shirt.

note: 'Kegiatan' means activity or event; commonly used for daily routines or organized events; related words: 'aktivitas' (more formal/borrowed), 'acara' (event/program).

sentences.text: Kegiatan hari ini adalah memasak bersama.
sentences.en: Today's activity is cooking together.

sentences.text: Saya suka kegiatan di luar rumah.
sentences.en: I like activities outside the house.

sentences.text: Anak-anak punya kegiatan di sekolah hari ini.
sentences.en: The children have an activity at school today.

note: 'Kolam renang' literally means 'swimming pool'; 'kolam' alone means pond or pool, while 'renang' means swimming — often confused with 'pantai' (beach) for outdoor swimming.

sentences.text: Saya suka berenang di kolam renang.
sentences.en: I like swimming in the swimming pool.

sentences.text: Hotel ini punya kolam renang yang besar.
sentences.en: This hotel has a big swimming pool.

sentences.text: Anak-anak bermain di kolam renang.
sentences.en: The children are playing in the swimming pool.

english: to do something, to undertake something, to make (a trip, effort)
note: "Melakukan" is the formal/written form; "lakukan" is the imperative or informal root; commonly used with activities, actions, and trips — not interchangeable with "membuat" (to make/create objects).

sentences.text: Saya melakukan perjalanan ke Bali besok.
sentences.en: I am making a trip to Bali tomorrow.

sentences.text: Dia melakukan pekerjaan rumah setiap hari.
sentences.en: She does housework every day.

sentences.text: Tolong lakukan tugas ini sekarang.
sentences.en: Please do this task now.

note: "Lari pagi" literally means "morning run/jog" and is a very common everyday phrase in Indonesia; often used interchangeably with "jogging pagi"; the word order is verb + time, which is typical in Indonesian.

sentences.text: Saya suka lari pagi di pantai.
sentences.en: I like jogging in the morning at the beach.

sentences.text: Dia lari pagi setiap hari Minggu.
sentences.en: She goes for a morning jog every Sunday.

sentences.text: Ayo lari pagi bersama saya!
sentences.en: Let's go for a morning jog together!

note: 'Lu' means 'you' in Jakarta/urban Indonesian slang (informal); avoid in formal settings — use 'Anda' or 'kamu' instead.

sentences.text: Lu mau makan di mana malam ini?
sentences.en: Where do you want to eat tonight?

sentences.text: Ini untuk lu, bukan untuk dia.
sentences.en: This is for you, not for him/her.

sentences.text: Lu tinggal di Bali ya?
sentences.en: You live in Bali, right?

note: 'Makasih' is an informal shortening of 'terima kasih' (thank you); use with friends or peers, not in formal settings.

sentences.text: Makasih ya, kamu sudah bantu aku.
sentences.en: Thanks, you already helped me.

sentences.text: Makasih banyak untuk kopinya!
sentences.en: Thanks a lot for the coffee!

sentences.text: Wah, makasih hadiahnya, aku suka!
sentences.en: Wow, thanks for the gift, I love it!

english: prayer room (for Muslims), a small mosque
note: 'Musala' is a small prayer room found in malls, offices, and schools; less formal than 'masjid' (mosque); also spelled 'musholla' or 'mushalla'.

sentences.text: Di mana musala di sini?
sentences.en: Where is the prayer room here?

sentences.text: Saya sholat di musala sekolah.
sentences.en: I pray at the school prayer room.

sentences.text: Musala ini bersih dan nyaman.
sentences.en: This prayer room is clean and comfortable.

english: why? why on earth...?, what (is someone) doing?, what for? what's the point?, what's going on?
note: 'Ngapain' is informal/colloquial Indonesian used to question someone's action or purpose; avoid in formal settings; related to 'kenapa' (why) and 'apa' (what).

sentences.text: Ngapain kamu di sini sendirian?
sentences.en: What are you doing here alone?

sentences.text: Kamu ngapain di pasar pagi ini?
sentences.en: What are you doing at the market this morning?

sentences.text: Ngapain beli itu, mahal sekali!
sentences.en: Why on earth buy that, it's so expensive!

note: 'Nih' is a casual spoken particle meaning 'here/this' or used to draw attention; very common in informal speech, avoid in formal writing.

sentences.text: Ini kopi nih, silakan diminum.
sentences.en: Here's the coffee, please drink it.

sentences.text: Aku lagi di pantai nih sekarang.
sentences.en: I'm at the beach right now.

sentences.text: Baju nih bagus banget, kan?
sentences.en: This shirt is really nice, right?

note: 'Olahraga' means sport or exercise as a general concept; used for both the activity and the noun (e.g., 'saya suka olahraga' = I like sport/exercise); related: 'berolahraga' (to exercise).

sentences.text: Saya suka olahraga setiap pagi.
sentences.en: I like to exercise every morning.

sentences.text: Olahraga itu bagus untuk kesehatan.
sentences.en: Sport is good for health.

sentences.text: Anak-anak bermain olahraga di sekolah.
sentences.en: The children play sport at school.

english: to be going steady, to be dating, to be going out with
note: "Pacaran" is casual/informal speech for being in a romantic relationship; commonly confused with "menikah" (to marry); related words: "pacar" (boyfriend/girlfriend), "jomblo" (single).

sentences.text: Mereka sudah pacaran selama dua tahun.
sentences.en: They have been dating for two years.

sentences.text: Apakah kamu sedang pacaran sekarang?
sentences.en: Are you currently in a relationship?

sentences.text: Dia tidak mau pacaran dulu.
sentences.en: She does not want to date yet.

note: "Sesudah" means "after" and is interchangeable with "setelah"; both are common, but "sesudah" is slightly more informal; not to be confused with "sebelum" (before).

sentences.text: Saya mandi sesudah olahraga pagi.
sentences.en: I shower after morning exercise.

sentences.text: Dia tidur sesudah makan malam.
sentences.en: She sleeps after dinner.

sentences.text: Kami pergi ke pantai sesudah hujan.
sentences.en: We go to the beach after the rain.

note: 'Sulit' means difficult or hard to do; similar to 'susah' (more informal/colloquial), while 'sulit' is slightly more formal; both are widely used in everyday speech.

sentences.text: Soal matematika ini sangat sulit untuk saya.
sentences.en: This math problem is very difficult for me.

sentences.text: Bahasa Bali sulit dipelajari oleh turis.
sentences.en: Balinese language is difficult to learn for tourists.

sentences.text: Mencari taksi di sini sangat sulit.
sentences.en: Finding a taxi here is very difficult.

note: 'Taman' means park or garden; commonly used in place names like 'Taman Mini'; not to be confused with 'kebun' which means a cultivated garden or yard.

sentences.text: Saya suka bermain di taman setiap sore.
sentences.en: I like to play in the park every afternoon.

sentences.text: Taman ini sangat indah dan bersih.
sentences.en: This park is very beautiful and clean.

sentences.text: Anak-anak berlari di taman bersama teman.
sentences.en: The children run in the park with friends.

english: a day off, a (day off for a) holiday, a one-day holiday
note: "Hari libur" refers to a single day off or holiday; for a longer vacation use "liburan"; commonly used for public holidays and days off work or school.

sentences.text: Besok adalah hari libur nasional.
sentences.en: Tomorrow is a national holiday.

sentences.text: Saya tidak kerja pada hari libur.
sentences.en: I don't work on a day off.

sentences.text: Anak-anak senang saat hari libur.
sentences.en: Children are happy when it is a holiday.

note: "Kalau (kamu/Anda) bagaimana?" is casual-to-neutral for "What about you?"; use "kamu" with friends and "Anda" in formal settings; often shortened to just "kalau kamu?" in conversation.

sentences.text: Saya suka nasi goreng, kalau kamu bagaimana?
sentences.en: I like fried rice, what about you?

sentences.text: Dia sudah makan, kalau Anda bagaimana?
sentences.en: She has already eaten, what about you?

sentences.text: Saya mau ke pantai, kalau Budi bagaimana?
sentences.en: I want to go to the beach, what about Budi?

english: definitely, sure to be, bound to (be...), must be (i.e. bound to be)
note: "Pasti" is used in everyday speech to express certainty; similar to "tentu" but more casual and very common in informal contexts.

sentences.text: Dia pasti datang ke pesta besok.
sentences.en: She will definitely come to the party tomorrow.

sentences.text: Makanan ini pasti enak sekali.
sentences.en: This food must be very delicious.

sentences.text: Kamu pasti lelah setelah perjalanan jauh.
sentences.en: You must be tired after the long trip.

note: 'Sekeluarga' means 'the whole family' as one unit; related to 'keluarga' (family), the prefix 'se-' means 'whole/entire'; used in everyday spoken Indonesian.

sentences.text: Kami pergi ke pantai sekeluarga.
sentences.en: We went to the beach as a whole family.

sentences.text: Mereka makan malam sekeluarga di rumah.
sentences.en: They had dinner together as a whole family at home.

sentences.text: Kami berlibur ke Bali sekeluarga.
sentences.en: We vacationed in Bali as a whole family.

note: 'Sepi' means quiet/lonely/deserted; use it for places or feelings, not sound levels (use 'tenang' for calm, 'sunyi' is a more literary synonym).

sentences.text: Pantai ini sangat sepi pagi ini.
sentences.en: This beach is very deserted this morning.

sentences.text: Aku merasa sepi di rumah sendirian.
sentences.en: I feel lonely at home alone.

sentences.text: Pasar itu sepi karena hari hujan.
sentences.en: The market is deserted because it is raining.

english: to really like, to enjoy, to love (doing something)
note: "Suka sekali" is informal/neutral and means you really like something; stronger than "suka" alone; often confused with "sangat suka" which means the same thing; related: "senang sekali" (very happy/pleased).

sentences.text: Saya suka sekali makan nasi goreng.
sentences.en: I really love eating fried rice.

sentences.text: Dia suka sekali pergi ke pantai.
sentences.en: She really loves going to the beach.

sentences.text: Kami suka sekali minum kopi Bali.
sentences.en: We really enjoy drinking Balinese coffee.

english: not allowed to, shouldn't, can't (i.e. not permitted to)
note: "Tidak boleh" expresses prohibition or not being permitted; stronger than "jangan" (don't) and commonly confused with "tidak bisa" (can't/unable to) — use "tidak boleh" for rules or permission, not ability.

sentences.text: Kamu tidak boleh makan di sini.
sentences.en: You are not allowed to eat here.

sentences.text: Anak-anak tidak boleh masuk ke sana.
sentences.en: Children are not allowed to enter there.

sentences.text: Kita tidak boleh berenang di sini.
sentences.en: We are not allowed to swim here.

english: free time, spare time, leisure time
note: 'Waktu senggang' is neutral/everyday register for free or leisure time; similar to 'waktu luang', which is also common and interchangeable in casual speech.

sentences.text: Saya suka membaca buku di waktu senggang.
sentences.en: I like to read books in my free time.

sentences.text: Apa yang kamu lakukan di waktu senggang?
sentences.en: What do you do in your spare time?

sentences.text: Di waktu senggang, saya pergi ke pantai.
sentences.en: In my free time, I go to the beach.

note: "Anggur" means both "wine" and "grape" in Indonesian; context usually clarifies which is meant.

sentences.text: Saya minum anggur merah di restoran.
sentences.en: I drink red wine at the restaurant.

sentences.text: Apakah kamu suka anggur putih?
sentences.en: Do you like white wine?

sentences.text: Kami pesan satu botol anggur.
sentences.en: We order one bottle of wine.

note: 'Bulu tangkis' is the standard Indonesian word for badminton; 'bulutangkis' (one word) is also accepted; very popular sport in Indonesia.

sentences.text: Saya suka bermain bulu tangkis setiap sore.
sentences.en: I like playing badminton every afternoon.

sentences.text: Adi dan Budi bermain bulu tangkis bersama.
sentences.en: Adi and Budi play badminton together.

sentences.text: Lapangan bulu tangkis ada di sana.
sentences.en: The badminton court is over there.

note: 'Capai' means tired/exhausted in informal Indonesian; similar to 'lelah' but more colloquial and common in everyday speech.

sentences.text: Saya sangat capai setelah bekerja hari ini.
sentences.en: I am very tired after working today.

sentences.text: Dia capai karena berjalan jauh.
sentences.en: She is tired because she walked far.

sentences.text: Kami capai dan ingin istirahat sekarang.
sentences.en: We are tired and want to rest now.

english: glass (i.e. a tumbler you drink from), a drinking glass
note: "Gelas" means a drinking glass or tumbler; don't confuse with "kaca" (glass the material) or "cangkir" (a cup with a handle, like a teacup).

sentences.text: Tolong ambilkan gelas untuk saya.
sentences.en: Please get a glass for me.

sentences.text: Gelas ini berisi air dingin.
sentences.en: This glass contains cold water.

sentences.text: Saya mau minum dari gelas biru.
sentences.en: I want to drink from the blue glass.

note: 'Kelab malam' is the standard Indonesian term for night club; slightly formal, also heard as 'klub malam' in casual speech.

sentences.text: Dia pergi ke kelab malam tadi malam.
sentences.en: He went to the night club last night.

sentences.text: Kelab malam itu tutup sekarang.
sentences.en: That night club is closed now.

sentences.text: Saya tidak suka kelab malam.
sentences.en: I don't like night clubs.

english: just a moment, wait a moment, hang on a sec
note: 'Nanti dulu' is a casual, polite way to ask someone to wait a moment; more informal than 'tunggu sebentar' and very common in everyday speech.

sentences.text: Nanti dulu, saya ambil dompet saya.
sentences.en: Just a moment, I'll get my wallet.

sentences.text: Nanti dulu, saya belum siap.
sentences.en: Hang on a sec, I'm not ready yet.

sentences.text: Nanti dulu, ibu masih memasak.
sentences.en: Wait a moment, mom is still cooking.

note: 'Percaya' means 'to believe' or 'to trust'; often used as 'saya percaya' (I believe) or 'percaya diri' (self-confident); do not confuse with 'mengerti' (to understand).

sentences.text: Saya percaya kamu bisa melakukannya.
sentences.en: I believe you can do it.

sentences.text: Dia tidak percaya cerita itu.
sentences.en: She does not believe that story.

sentences.text: Kami percaya pada teman kami.
sentences.en: We trust our friend.

english: all, all of them, everyone, everybody
note: 'Semua' means 'all/everyone' and is used before nouns or alone; it is more common in everyday speech than 'seluruh' (which sounds more formal).

sentences.text: Semua anak-anak bermain di pantai.
sentences.en: All the children are playing at the beach.

sentences.text: Ibu membeli semua buah di pasar.
sentences.en: Mom bought all the fruit at the market.

sentences.text: Semua orang suka nasi goreng.
sentences.en: Everyone likes fried rice.

note: 'Tadi malam' means 'last night' and refers to the previous night; don't confuse with 'kemarin malam' which is also used but less common in casual speech.

sentences.text: Saya makan nasi goreng tadi malam.
sentences.en: I ate fried rice last night.

sentences.text: Tadi malam hujan sangat deras.
sentences.en: Last night it rained very heavily.

sentences.text: Dia tidur lebih awal tadi malam.
sentences.en: He slept earlier last night.

english: so ... after all, it turns out that ... after all
note: 'Ternyata' expresses surprise at a newly discovered fact; used in casual speech; similar to 'oh ternyata' (oh, so it turns out); related: 'rupanya' (it seems).

sentences.text: Ternyata dia tinggal di Bali.
sentences.en: It turns out he lives in Bali.

sentences.text: Makanan ini ternyata sangat enak!
sentences.en: This food turns out to be very delicious!

sentences.text: Ternyata toko itu sudah tutup.
sentences.en: It turns out that shop is already closed.

note: 'Wiski' is a loanword from English 'whisky'; used in casual/adult contexts; related words: 'bir' (beer), 'anggur' (wine), 'minuman keras' (alcohol).

sentences.text: Dia memesan wiski di bar itu.
sentences.en: He ordered whisky at that bar.

sentences.text: Wiski ini sangat mahal harganya.
sentences.en: This whisky is very expensive.

sentences.text: Saya tidak suka minum wiski.
sentences.en: I don't like drinking whisky.

note: 'Besok' means 'tomorrow'; very common in daily speech; related words: 'kemarin' (yesterday), 'hari ini' (today).

sentences.text: Besok saya pergi ke pasar.
sentences.en: Tomorrow I am going to the market.

sentences.text: Kita makan bersama besok ya?
sentences.en: We eat together tomorrow, okay?

sentences.text: Besok ada upacara di pura.
sentences.en: Tomorrow there is a ceremony at the temple.

note: 'Hari ini' means 'today'; 'hari' alone means 'day', and 'ini' means 'this' — together they form a common time expression used in everyday speech.

sentences.text: Hari ini saya pergi ke pasar.
sentences.en: Today I go to the market.

sentences.text: Cuaca hari ini sangat panas.
sentences.en: The weather today is very hot.

sentences.text: Hari ini kami makan nasi goreng.
sentences.en: Today we eat fried rice.

note: "Kemarin" means "yesterday" and is used in everyday speech; do not confuse with "kemarin dulu" (the day before yesterday) or "besok" (tomorrow).

sentences.text: Kemarin saya makan nasi goreng di warung.
sentences.en: Yesterday I ate fried rice at the warung.

sentences.text: Dia pergi ke pantai kemarin pagi.
sentences.en: She went to the beach yesterday morning.

sentences.text: Kemarin hujan deras sekali di sini.
sentences.en: Yesterday it rained very heavily here.

note: "hari Minggu" means Sunday; "hari" means day, used before all day names (e.g. hari Senin = Monday); always capitalized.

sentences.text: Saya pergi ke pantai pada hari Minggu.
sentences.en: I go to the beach on Sunday.

sentences.text: Hari Minggu adalah hari libur.
sentences.en: Sunday is a holiday.

sentences.text: Kita makan bersama keluarga hari Minggu.
sentences.en: We eat together with family on Sunday.

note: 'hari Senin' means Monday; 'hari' means 'day' and is used before all day names in Indonesian; similar to 'hari Selasa' (Tuesday), 'hari Rabu' (Wednesday), etc.

sentences.text: Saya pergi ke sekolah pada hari Senin.
sentences.en: I go to school on Monday.

sentences.text: Pasar buka pada hari Senin pagi.
sentences.en: The market opens on Monday morning.

sentences.text: Hari Senin adalah hari kerja.
sentences.en: Monday is a workday.

note: 'Hari Selasa' means Tuesday; 'hari' means 'day' and can be dropped in casual speech; days of the week in Indonesian come from Arabic (Selasa = Tuesday, from 'thulāthāʾ').

sentences.text: Hari Selasa saya pergi ke pasar.
sentences.en: On Tuesday I go to the market.

sentences.text: Besok adalah hari Selasa.
sentences.en: Tomorrow is Tuesday.

sentences.text: Kelas bahasa Inggris ada hari Selasa.
sentences.en: The English class is on Tuesday.

note: 'Hari Rabu' means Wednesday; 'hari' means 'day' and is often included but can be dropped in casual speech.

sentences.text: Hari Rabu saya pergi ke pasar.
sentences.en: On Wednesday I go to the market.

sentences.text: Kelas bahasa Inggris ada hari Rabu.
sentences.en: The English class is on Wednesday.

sentences.text: Besok adalah hari Rabu.
sentences.en: Tomorrow is Wednesday.

note: "Hari Kamis" means Thursday; "hari" means day, used before all day names in Indonesian (hari Senin, hari Selasa, etc.).

sentences.text: Saya pergi ke pasar pada hari Kamis.
sentences.en: I go to the market on Thursday.

sentences.text: Kelas bahasa Inggris ada pada hari Kamis.
sentences.en: English class is on Thursday.

sentences.text: Hari Kamis saya libur dari sekolah.
sentences.en: On Thursday I have a day off from school.

note: 'Hari Jumat' means Friday; 'hari' means 'day', and days of the week always use 'hari' before the name.

sentences.text: Saya pergi ke pasar pada hari Jumat.
sentences.en: I go to the market on Friday.

sentences.text: Hari Jumat adalah hari favorit saya.
sentences.en: Friday is my favorite day.

sentences.text: Kita makan bersama pada hari Jumat.
sentences.en: We eat together on Friday.

note: 'hari Sabtu' means Saturday; 'hari' means 'day', often omitted in casual speech; related: hari Minggu (Sunday), hari Senin (Monday).

sentences.text: Saya pergi ke pasar pada hari Sabtu.
sentences.en: I go to the market on Saturday.

sentences.text: Besok adalah hari Sabtu.
sentences.en: Tomorrow is Saturday.

sentences.text: Kami libur pada hari Sabtu.
sentences.en: We have a day off on Saturday.

note: 'Kapan' means 'when' used in questions about time; commonly confused with 'ketika' (when/while, used in statements, not questions).

sentences.text: Kapan kamu pergi ke Bali?
sentences.en: When are you going to Bali?

sentences.text: Kapan warung ini buka setiap hari?
sentences.en: When does this food stall open every day?

sentences.text: Ibu mau tahu kapan kita makan.
sentences.en: Mom wants to know when we are eating.

note: 'Agen perjalanan' is the formal/standard term for travel agent; informally people may just say 'travel' or 'agen travel'.

sentences.text: Saya pergi ke agen perjalanan hari ini.
sentences.en: I am going to the travel agent today.

sentences.text: Agen perjalanan itu menjual tiket pesawat murah.
sentences.en: That travel agent sells cheap plane tickets.

sentences.text: Ibu membeli paket wisata di agen perjalanan.
sentences.en: Mom bought a tour package at the travel agent.

note: 'Jadwal' means schedule or timetable; commonly used for class schedules, bus times, and work shifts; related words: 'jadwal pelajaran' (school timetable), 'terjadwal' (scheduled).

sentences.text: Jadwal kelas saya mulai jam delapan.
sentences.en: My class schedule starts at eight o'clock.

sentences.text: Apa jadwal bus ke Denpasar?
sentences.en: What is the bus schedule to Denpasar?

sentences.text: Saya lupa membawa jadwal hari ini.
sentences.en: I forgot to bring my schedule today.

note: "Menurut" means "according to" and is used before a source or person's opinion; beginners often confuse it with "menurut saya" (in my opinion).

sentences.text: Menurut ibu, warung ini enak sekali.
sentences.en: According to mom, this food stall is very delicious.

sentences.text: Menurut peta, pantai itu dekat sini.
sentences.en: According to the map, that beach is near here.

sentences.text: Menurut saya, harga ini terlalu mahal.
sentences.en: In my opinion, this price is too expensive.

note: 'Penerbangan' means a flight or aviation; commonly used at airports; related words: 'terbang' (to fly), 'pesawat' (airplane).

sentences.text: Penerbangan saya ke Bali besok pagi.
sentences.en: My flight to Bali is tomorrow morning.

sentences.text: Berapa lama penerbangan dari Jakarta ke Bali?
sentences.en: How long is the flight from Jakarta to Bali?

sentences.text: Penerbangan itu terlambat dua jam.
sentences.en: That flight was two hours late.

note: 'Tiket' is a loanword from Dutch/English, used for tickets of all kinds (transport, events); very common in everyday speech.

sentences.text: Saya beli tiket bus ke Denpasar.
sentences.en: I buy a bus ticket to Denpasar.

sentences.text: Berapa harga tiket masuk ke pantai?
sentences.en: How much is the entrance ticket to the beach?

sentences.text: Dia sudah pesan tiket kereta api.
sentences.en: She has already booked a train ticket.

english: to (when you are talking about something that is directed towards an individual or a group of people, not a place)
note: "kepada" means "to" when directing something at a person or group (not a place); often confused with "ke" which is used for places/directions.

sentences.text: Dia memberi hadiah kepada ibunya.
sentences.en: She gives a gift to her mother.

sentences.text: Saya berterima kasih kepada guru saya.
sentences.en: I am thankful to my teacher.

sentences.text: Ibu berbicara kepada anak-anak.
sentences.en: Mother speaks to the children.

note: 'Majalah' means magazine; commonly confused with 'koran' (newspaper); related word: 'buku' (book).

sentences.text: Saya membaca majalah di rumah.
sentences.en: I read a magazine at home.

sentences.text: Dia membeli majalah di toko.
sentences.en: She buys a magazine at the shop.

sentences.text: Majalah ini sangat menarik.
sentences.en: This magazine is very interesting.

note: 'Membaca' is the formal/full form; 'baca' is the informal root, often used in casual speech and commands (e.g., 'Baca ini!'); related words: 'bacaan' (reading material), 'pembaca' (reader).

sentences.text: Saya suka membaca buku setiap hari.
sentences.en: I like to read books every day.

sentences.text: Dia membaca koran di warung kopi.
sentences.en: He/She reads the newspaper at the coffee shop.

note: "Membersihkan" is the formal/full form; "bersihkan" is the imperative or informal shortening; both mean 'to clean something' (transitive), unlike "bersih" which is just the adjective 'clean'.

sentences.text: Tolong bersihkan meja sebelum makan.
sentences.en: Please clean the table before eating.

sentences.text: Ibu membersihkan kamar setiap pagi.
sentences.en: Mom cleans the room every morning.

sentences.text: Ayo membersihkan pantai bersama-sama!
sentences.en: Let's clean the beach together!

note: 'Mencuci' is the formal verb form; 'cuci' is used in casual speech (e.g., 'cuci tangan' = wash hands); common phrases include 'cuci piring' (wash dishes) and 'cuci baju' (wash clothes).

sentences.text: Saya mencuci tangan sebelum makan.
sentences.en: I wash my hands before eating.

sentences.text: Ibu cuci baju setiap pagi.
sentences.en: Mom washes clothes every morning.

sentences.text: Kami mencuci piring setelah makan malam.
sentences.en: We wash the dishes after dinner.

note: 'Mendengarkan' is the formal/full form; 'dengarkan' is the imperative form used in commands; both mean to actively listen to something, unlike 'mendengar' which means to simply hear.

sentences.text: Saya suka mendengarkan musik di rumah.
sentences.en: I like to listen to music at home.

sentences.text: Tolong dengarkan guru di kelas.
sentences.en: Please listen to the teacher in class.

sentences.text: Dia mendengarkan radio setiap pagi.
sentences.en: She listens to the radio every morning.

english: to watch something (especially TV, a sports match, a performance, a movie, a spectacle)
note: "Menonton" is the formal/base form; "nonton" is the casual spoken form commonly used in everyday conversation; often used for watching TV, films, or live events, not for watching over a person (use "melihat" or "memperhatikan" for that).

sentences.text: Saya ingin menonton film di bioskop.
sentences.en: I want to watch a movie at the cinema.

sentences.text: Kami menonton pertandingan bola bersama.
sentences.en: We watch the football match together.

sentences.text: Dia suka menonton TV setiap malam.
sentences.en: She likes to watch TV every night.

note: "Menulis" is the active verb form (me- prefix on root "tulis"); used in formal and everyday contexts for writing by hand or typing.

sentences.text: Saya menulis surat untuk ibu saya.
sentences.en: I am writing a letter for my mother.

sentences.text: Dia menulis nama di buku.
sentences.en: She writes her name in the book.

sentences.text: Anak itu belajar menulis di sekolah.
sentences.en: That child is learning to write at school.

note: "Menyapu" is the active verb form (me- prefix + sapu); the base word "sapu" also means broom, so context clarifies meaning.

sentences.text: Ibu menyapu lantai setiap pagi.
sentences.en: Mom sweeps the floor every morning.

sentences.text: Saya menyapu halaman rumah sekarang.
sentences.en: I am sweeping the yard now.

sentences.text: Adik menyapu dapur dengan bersih.
sentences.en: My younger sibling sweeps the kitchen cleanly.

note: 'Novel' is used the same as in English; it refers to a fiction book, commonly confused with 'buku' (book) in general.

sentences.text: Saya membaca novel di kamar.
sentences.en: I am reading a novel in the room.

sentences.text: Novel ini sangat menarik dan seru.
sentences.en: This novel is very interesting and exciting.

sentences.text: Dia membeli novel baru kemarin.
sentences.en: She bought a new novel yesterday.

note: 'Piring' means plate or dish; 'cuci piring' means to wash the dishes; do not confuse with 'mangkuk' (bowl).

sentences.text: Tolong ambilkan piring untuk makan malam.
sentences.en: Please get a plate for dinner.

sentences.text: Saya mencuci piring setelah makan.
sentences.en: I wash the dishes after eating.

sentences.text: Di meja ada dua piring bersih.
sentences.en: On the table there are two clean plates.

note: 'Sapu' means broom as a noun; 'menyapu' is the verb form meaning to sweep — avoid confusing the two.

sentences.text: Ibu menggunakan sapu untuk membersihkan lantai.
sentences.en: Mom uses a broom to clean the floor.

sentences.text: Di mana sapu itu?
sentences.en: Where is the broom?

sentences.text: Anak itu memegang sapu besar.
sentences.en: That child is holding a big broom.

english: what are (you) doing?, what is (he/she) doing?
note: "Sedang apa?" is casual spoken Indonesian for asking what someone is currently doing; "sedang" marks ongoing action like English "-ing"; often shortened to "lagi apa?" in informal speech.

sentences.text: Kamu sedang apa di rumah?
sentences.en: What are you doing at home?

sentences.text: Ibu sedang apa sekarang?
sentences.en: What is Mom doing now?

sentences.text: Dia sedang apa di pasar?
sentences.en: What is he/she doing at the market?

note: 'Surat kabar' is the formal/written word for newspaper; the informal word 'koran' is more common in everyday speech.

sentences.text: Ayah membaca surat kabar setiap pagi.
sentences.en: Father reads the newspaper every morning.

sentences.text: Saya membeli surat kabar di warung.
sentences.en: I buy a newspaper at the small shop.

sentences.text: Ada berita bagus di surat kabar.
sentences.en: There is good news in the newspaper.

english: a letter (i.e. an item of correspondence)
note: 'Surat' means a physical or written letter/document; also used in 'surat kabar' (newspaper) and 'surat izin' (permit); do not confuse with 'huruf' (a letter of the alphabet).

sentences.text: Saya menulis surat untuk ibu saya.
sentences.en: I am writing a letter to my mother.

sentences.text: Ada surat di atas meja.
sentences.en: There is a letter on the table.

sentences.text: Dia mengirim surat ke temannya.
sentences.en: He sends a letter to his friend.

note: 'Bangun' means 'to wake up / get out of bed'; don't confuse with 'bangun' meaning 'to build' — context makes it clear; often used with 'tidur' (sleep).

sentences.text: Saya bangun pukul enam setiap pagi.
sentences.en: I get up at six every morning.

sentences.text: Dia tidak mau bangun dari tempat tidur.
sentences.en: He doesn't want to get up from the bed.

sentences.text: Ayo bangun, sudah siang!
sentences.en: Come on, get up — it's already late morning!

note: 'Berita' means 'news' (neutral/formal register); commonly heard in 'berita hari ini' (today's news); related: 'kabar' (informal news/update).

sentences.text: Saya menonton berita di televisi setiap malam.
sentences.en: I watch the news on television every night.

sentences.text: Berita itu sangat mengejutkan saya.
sentences.en: That news really surprised me.

sentences.text: Dia membaca berita pagi ini.
sentences.en: She reads the news this morning.

english: to get dressed, to be dressed
note: 'Berpakaian' means to dress or be dressed; related to 'pakaian' (clothing); used in both active and descriptive contexts.

sentences.text: Anak itu berpakaian rapi untuk ke sekolah.
sentences.en: The child is dressed neatly to go to school.

sentences.text: Dia berpakaian merah hari ini.
sentences.en: She is dressed in red today.

sentences.text: Saya harus berpakaian bersih setiap hari.
sentences.en: I must dress cleanly every day.

english: to get ready, to make preparations, to prepare (for something)
note: Informal/neutral register; 'bersiap-siap' implies repeated or ongoing preparation, similar to 'bersiap' but more emphatic; related: 'siap' (ready), 'mempersiapkan' (to prepare something).

sentences.text: Kami bersiap-siap sebelum pergi ke pantai.
sentences.en: We are getting ready before going to the beach.

sentences.text: Dia bersiap-siap untuk pergi ke sekolah.
sentences.en: She is getting ready to go to school.

sentences.text: Ayo bersiap-siap, bus sudah datang!
sentences.en: Let's get ready, the bus is already here!

note: 'Bersisir' means to comb one's own hair (reflexive); related word: 'sisir' (noun: comb).

sentences.text: Saya bersisir sebelum pergi ke sekolah.
sentences.en: I comb my hair before going to school.

sentences.text: Adik bersisir di depan cermin.
sentences.en: My younger sibling combs their hair in front of the mirror.

sentences.text: Ibu bersisir setiap pagi hari.
sentences.en: Mom combs her hair every morning.

note: "Menggosok gigi" literally means "rubbing/scrubbing teeth"; commonly said morning and night routines; related: "sikat gigi" (toothbrush), "pasta gigi" (toothpaste).

sentences.text: Saya menggosok gigi setiap pagi.
sentences.en: I brush my teeth every morning.

sentences.text: Ibu menyuruh saya menggosok gigi sekarang.
sentences.en: Mom tells me to brush my teeth now.

sentences.text: Anak itu menggosok gigi sebelum tidur.
sentences.en: That child brushes their teeth before sleeping.

note: 'Kemudian' means 'then/after that' and is slightly more formal than 'lalu'; both are common in everyday speech for sequencing events.

sentences.text: Saya makan nasi, kemudian minum air.
sentences.en: I eat rice, then drink water.

sentences.text: Dia pergi ke pasar, kemudian pulang.
sentences.en: She goes to the market, then goes home.

sentences.text: Kami mandi, kemudian tidur siang.
sentences.en: We shower, then take a nap.

note: 'Membeli' is the formal/written form; 'beli' is the casual spoken form — both mean 'to buy'; often confused with 'menjual' (to sell).

sentences.text: Saya ingin membeli nasi goreng di warung.
sentences.en: I want to buy nasi goreng at the food stall.

sentences.text: Dia beli oleh-oleh untuk keluarganya.
sentences.en: She buys souvenirs for her family.

sentences.text: Kami beli buah di pasar pagi ini.
sentences.en: We buy fruit at the market this morning.

english: to go and get something, to fetch something, to reach out and remove, to pick up something
note: "Mengambil" is the formal/active form; "ambil" is the casual imperative or base form — both very common in everyday speech.

sentences.text: Tolong ambil air dari dapur.
sentences.en: Please fetch some water from the kitchen.

sentences.text: Dia mengambil buku di atas meja.
sentences.en: He picks up the book on the table.

sentences.text: Saya mengambil tas saya di kamar.
sentences.en: I go and get my bag from the room.

note: "Pemandangan" is the noun form from root "pandang" (to look/gaze); commonly used for natural scenery like mountains, rice fields, or ocean views; not used for indoor scenes or art.

sentences.text: Pemandangan di Bali sangat indah sekali.
sentences.en: The scenery in Bali is very beautiful.

sentences.text: Saya suka pemandangan sawah dari sini.
sentences.en: I like the view of the rice fields from here.

sentences.text: Pemandangan laut itu sangat bagus.
sentences.en: That ocean view is very nice.

note: "Sebelum" means "before" in time or sequence; don't confuse with "sesudah" (after) or "setelah" (after/following).

sentences.text: Cuci tangan sebelum makan.
sentences.en: Wash your hands before eating.

sentences.text: Dia mandi sebelum pergi ke sekolah.
sentences.en: She showers before going to school.

sentences.text: Saya tidur sebelum jam sepuluh.
sentences.en: I sleep before ten o'clock.

english: self, by oneself (without help from anyone), alone
note: 'Sendiri' means alone, by oneself, or without help; often confused with 'saja' (just/only); related: 'diri sendiri' (oneself).

sentences.text: Dia pergi ke pasar sendiri.
sentences.en: She goes to the market alone.

sentences.text: Aku bisa makan sendiri, terima kasih.
sentences.en: I can eat by myself, thank you.

sentences.text: Anak itu tidur sendiri di kamar.
sentences.en: That child sleeps alone in the room.

note: 'Alat' is a neutral, everyday word for tools or devices; 'alat tulis' means stationery, 'alat musik' means musical instrument — it combines freely with other nouns.

sentences.text: Saya butuh alat untuk memasak nasi.
sentences.en: I need a tool to cook rice.

sentences.text: Alat musik ini sangat indah.
sentences.en: This musical instrument is very beautiful.

sentences.text: Di mana alat tulis saya?
sentences.en: Where is my stationery?

english: a shirt, a dress, an upper-body garment, (also loosely: clothes)
note: 'Baju' broadly means any upper-body garment or clothing; closely related to 'pakaian' (clothing in general) and 'kemeja' (a formal shirt specifically).

sentences.text: Saya memakai baju merah hari ini.
sentences.en: I am wearing a red shirt today.

sentences.text: Baju adik saya ada di sana.
sentences.en: My younger sibling's clothes are over there.

sentences.text: Ibu membeli baju baru di pasar.
sentences.en: Mom bought a new dress at the market.

note: 'Elektronik' is a neutral everyday word used as an adjective or noun; commonly seen in store signs like 'toko elektronik' (electronics store); related: 'listrik' (electricity/electric).

sentences.text: Toko elektronik itu menjual televisi baru.
sentences.en: That electronics store sells new televisions.

sentences.text: Ayah membeli peralatan elektronik di pasar.
sentences.en: Dad bought electronic equipment at the market.

sentences.text: Barang elektronik ini mahal sekali.
sentences.en: This electronic item is very expensive.

note: 'Habis' literally means 'finished/run out', but informally it means 'after'; don't confuse with 'sesudah' (formal) or 'setelah' (also formal).

sentences.text: Habis makan, aku minum kopi.
sentences.en: After eating, I drink coffee.

sentences.text: Habis sekolah, dia pulang ke rumah.
sentences.en: After school, he goes home.

sentences.text: Aku tidur habis nonton film.
sentences.en: I sleep after watching a movie.

note: 'Ingin' is a polite/neutral way to say 'want to' or 'wish to'; more formal than 'mau' but both are very common in everyday speech.

sentences.text: Saya ingin makan nasi goreng hari ini.
sentences.en: I want to eat fried rice today.

sentences.text: Dia ingin pergi ke pantai besok.
sentences.en: She wants to go to the beach tomorrow.

sentences.text: Kami ingin belajar bahasa Indonesia bersama.
sentences.en: We want to learn Indonesian together.

english: to happen, occur, transpire, take place
note: "Jadi" as a verb means something happened or took place; don't confuse with "jadi" meaning "so/therefore" or "become" — context determines meaning.

sentences.text: Pesta itu tidak jadi karena hujan deras.
sentences.en: The party did not take place because of heavy rain.

sentences.text: Apakah pertemuan besok jadi?
sentences.en: Will tomorrow's meeting take place?

sentences.text: Acara di pantai jadi kemarin malam.
sentences.en: The event at the beach took place last night.

english: we (including the person or persons you are talking to)
note: "kita" means "we/us" including the listener; contrast with "kami" which excludes the listener.

sentences.text: Kita pergi ke pantai bersama-sama.
sentences.en: We are going to the beach together.

sentences.text: Hari ini kita makan nasi goreng.
sentences.en: Today we eat fried rice.

sentences.text: Kita belajar bahasa Indonesia setiap hari.
sentences.en: We study Indonesian every day.

english: we (excluding the person or persons you are talking to)
note: "Kami" means "we/us" but excludes the listener; contrast with "kita" which includes everyone present.

sentences.text: Kami tinggal di Bali.
sentences.en: We live in Bali.

sentences.text: Kami makan nasi goreng tadi malam.
sentences.en: We ate fried rice last night.

sentences.text: Kami pergi ke pantai besok.
sentences.en: We are going to the beach tomorrow.

note: 'Keren' is casual/colloquial for cool, stylish, or awesome; avoid in formal writing; related: 'bagus' (good), 'hebat' (great).

sentences.text: Baju kamu sangat keren hari ini.
sentences.en: Your clothes are very stylish today.

sentences.text: Motor baru dia keren sekali.
sentences.en: His new motorcycle is very cool.

sentences.text: Rambut kamu keren, seperti artis.
sentences.en: Your hair is stylish, like a celebrity.

english: to try to do something, to try something out, to try on (clothes)
note: "Mencoba" is the formal verb form; "coba" is the casual/imperative form often used in speech; don't confuse with "mencicipi" (to taste food specifically).

sentences.text: Saya ingin mencoba baju baru itu.
sentences.en: I want to try on that new shirt.

sentences.text: Dia mencoba makanan khas Bali.
sentences.en: She is trying the typical Balinese food.

sentences.text: Coba sepatu ini dulu, ya!
sentences.en: Try on these shoes first, okay!

note: 'Minggu' means 'week' but also 'Sunday'; use context to tell them apart — e.g. 'hari Minggu' means Sunday, 'satu minggu' means one week.

sentences.text: Saya belajar bahasa Indonesia dua minggu.
sentences.en: I have been studying Indonesian for two weeks.

sentences.text: Kami pergi ke Bali minggu depan.
sentences.en: We are going to Bali next week.

sentences.text: Dia bekerja lima hari setiap minggu.
sentences.en: He works five days every week.

english: (informal) to go to the movies, to watch something (especially TV, a sports match, a parade etc.)
note: "Nonton" is the informal spoken form of "menonton"; use it for watching TV, films, or live events — not for reading or listening.

sentences.text: Aku mau nonton film di bioskop.
sentences.en: I want to watch a movie at the cinema.

sentences.text: Mereka nonton sepak bola bersama.
sentences.en: They watch football together.

sentences.text: Kamu mau nonton TV malam ini?
sentences.en: Do you want to watch TV tonight?

english: to arrive in/at (a place), to reach (a destination)
note: "Sampai di" means to arrive at a specific place; use "di" before place names, not "ke" (which shows direction/movement toward).

sentences.text: Kami sampai di Bali tadi pagi.
sentences.en: We arrived in Bali this morning.

sentences.text: Bus sampai di terminal jam tiga.
sentences.en: The bus arrived at the terminal at three o'clock.

sentences.text: Dia sampai di rumah sakit kemarin.
sentences.en: She arrived at the hospital yesterday.

note: "Yang lalu" follows a time word (e.g. minggu, bulan, tahun) to mean 'last' or 'ago'; do not confuse with "yang lain" (the other).

sentences.text: Saya pergi ke Bali minggu yang lalu.
sentences.en: I went to Bali last week.

sentences.text: Dia lahir tahun yang lalu.
sentences.en: She was born last year.

sentences.text: Kami makan nasi goreng kemarin yang lalu.
sentences.en: We ate fried rice the day before yesterday.

note: "Bahasa Belanda" means the Dutch language; "Belanda" alone refers to the Netherlands or Dutch people, similar to how "bahasa Inggris" means English.

sentences.text: Dia belajar bahasa Belanda di sekolah.
sentences.en: She studies Dutch at school.

sentences.text: Apakah kamu bisa berbicara bahasa Belanda?
sentences.en: Can you speak Dutch?

sentences.text: Bahasa Belanda sulit untuk dipelajari.
sentences.en: Dutch is difficult to learn.

english: to be in power, to be the dominant force
note: 'Berkuasa' means to hold power or be dominant; often used for leaders or rulers; related to 'kuasa' (power) and 'penguasa' (ruler/authority).

sentences.text: Raja itu berkuasa di seluruh kerajaan.
sentences.en: That king is in power over the entire kingdom.

sentences.text: Siapa yang berkuasa di desa ini?
sentences.en: Who is in power in this village?

sentences.text: Presiden berkuasa selama lima tahun.
sentences.en: The president is in power for five years.

note: 'Bikin' is an informal/colloquial synonym of 'membuat' (to make/create); very common in casual speech but avoid in formal writing.

sentences.text: Dia bikin kue untuk ulang tahun.
sentences.en: She makes a cake for the birthday.

sentences.text: Aku mau bikin nasi goreng sekarang.
sentences.en: I want to make fried rice now.

sentences.text: Tolong bikin kopi untuk tamu ya.
sentences.en: Please make coffee for the guest.

note: "Membuat" is the formal/written form; "buat" is the casual spoken shortform. Often confused with "memasak" (to cook), but "membuat" is broader—used for making any object or thing.

sentences.text: Saya membuat kue untuk keluarga saya.
sentences.en: I am making a cake for my family.

sentences.text: Dia buat minuman dingin di dapur.
sentences.en: She is making a cold drink in the kitchen.

sentences.text: Kami membuat kerajinan tangan di sekolah.
sentences.en: We are making handicrafts at school.

english: to sit around (in a casual or leisurely way)
note: Informal/casual reduplication of 'duduk'; implies relaxing or lounging, not purposeful sitting; similar to 'santai-santai' (hanging out lazily).

sentences.text: Mereka duduk-duduk di pantai sore ini.
sentences.en: They are sitting around at the beach this afternoon.

sentences.text: Aku suka duduk-duduk di teras rumah.
sentences.en: I like to sit around on the house porch.

sentences.text: Kami duduk-duduk sambil minum kopi.
sentences.en: We are sitting around while drinking coffee.

english: in former times, a long time ago, used to (i.e. regularly happened in former times)
note: "Dulu" meaning 'in former times / used to' refers to past habits or states; don't confuse with "dulu" meaning 'first/before someone else' — context makes the difference; related: "dahulu", "zaman dulu".

sentences.text: Dulu saya sering makan di warung itu.
sentences.en: I used to eat at that warung often.

sentences.text: Dulu jalan ini tidak ada lampu.
sentences.en: In former times, this road had no lights.

sentences.text: Nenek saya dulu tinggal di desa.
sentences.en: My grandmother used to live in a village.

english: law, the law (as a body of regulations or an area of study)
note: "Hukum" means law as a system or field of study; not used for a specific rule (use "peraturan" for that); related: "ahli hukum" (lawyer/legal expert).

sentences.text: Dia belajar hukum di universitas.
sentences.en: He studies law at university.

sentences.text: Semua orang harus ikut hukum.
sentences.en: Everyone must follow the law.

sentences.text: Hukum di Indonesia sangat penting.
sentences.en: The law in Indonesia is very important.

note: 'Ibu kos' means the woman who owns and manages a boarding house (kos); often called 'ibu' for short by tenants.

sentences.text: Ibu kos saya sangat baik hati.
sentences.en: My landlady is very kind.

sentences.text: Saya membayar uang kos ke ibu kos.
sentences.en: I pay the rent to the landlady.

sentences.text: Ibu kos memasak untuk para penghuni.
sentences.en: The landlady cooks for the residents.

note: "Kalo pagi" is informal spoken Indonesian (kalo = kalau/if/when); used in casual daily conversation, not formal writing.

sentences.text: Kalo pagi, saya suka minum kopi.
sentences.en: In the morning, I like to drink coffee.

sentences.text: Kalo pagi dia selalu jogging di pantai.
sentences.en: In the morning, he always jogs at the beach.

sentences.text: Kalo pagi udara di sini sejuk.
sentences.en: In the morning, the air here is cool.

note: "Karena" means "because" and introduces a reason; it is interchangeable with "sebab" but "karena" is more common in everyday speech.

sentences.text: Saya lapar karena belum makan siang.
sentences.en: I am hungry because I have not had lunch yet.

sentences.text: Dia senang karena cuaca hari ini cerah.
sentences.en: She is happy because the weather today is sunny.

sentences.text: Kami di rumah karena hujan deras.
sentences.en: We are at home because it is raining heavily.

note: "Kenapa?" means "why?" and is the most common casual form; "mengapa?" is more formal; both are interchangeable but "kenapa?" is used in everyday speech.

sentences.text: Kenapa kamu tidak makan nasi hari ini?
sentences.en: Why didn't you eat rice today?

sentences.text: Dia menangis, kenapa?
sentences.en: She is crying, why?

sentences.text: Kenapa toko ini tutup sekarang?
sentences.en: Why is this shop closed now?

english: all sorts (of), all kinds (of), various kinds of
note: 'Macam-macam' is informal/casual speech, interchangeable with 'berbagai' (more formal); often used in markets or describing variety; related: 'macam' means 'type/kind'.

sentences.text: Di pasar ada macam-macam buah segar.
sentences.en: At the market there are all kinds of fresh fruit.

sentences.text: Warung itu jual macam-macam makanan enak.
sentences.en: That small restaurant sells all sorts of delicious food.

sentences.text: Dia punya macam-macam baju batik.
sentences.en: She has various kinds of batik clothes.

english: a subject (of study at a university), a course, a unit of study
note: Used in university contexts only; for school subjects use 'mata pelajaran' instead; 'kuliah' alone means 'university lecture'.

sentences.text: Saya ambil mata kuliah bahasa Inggris.
sentences.en: I am taking an English course.

sentences.text: Mata kuliah ini sangat sulit.
sentences.en: This subject is very difficult.

sentences.text: Berapa mata kuliah kamu semester ini?
sentences.en: How many courses are you taking this semester?

note: 'Memberikan' is the formal/written form; 'berikan' is the shorter spoken imperative form; both mean 'to give something (to someone)'.

sentences.text: Ibu memberikan nasi kepada anak itu.
sentences.en: Mother gives rice to that child.

sentences.text: Tolong berikan air minum kepada saya.
sentences.en: Please give me some drinking water.

sentences.text: Pak guru memberikan buku baru hari ini.
sentences.en: The teacher gives a new book today.

note: "Mengapa?" means "why?" and is slightly formal; the casual everyday version is "kenapa?" — both are correct but "kenapa?" is more common in spoken Indonesian.

sentences.text: Mengapa kamu tidak makan nasi hari ini?
sentences.en: Why did you not eat rice today?

sentences.text: Mengapa toko itu tutup sekarang?
sentences.en: Why is that shop closed now?

note: 'Ngorok' is informal/colloquial for snoring; use 'mendengkur' in formal writing; often used humorously among friends and family.

sentences.text: Ayah saya ngorok setiap malam.
sentences.en: My father snores every night.

sentences.text: Kucing itu tidur dan ngorok keras.
sentences.en: That cat sleeps and snores loudly.

sentences.text: Kamu ngorok tadi malam, lho!
sentences.en: You were snoring last night, you know!

note: 'Pagi-pagi' means very early in the morning; reduplication of 'pagi' intensifies meaning; often used in casual speech.

sentences.text: Saya bangun pagi-pagi untuk pergi ke pasar.
sentences.en: I wake up very early in the morning to go to the market.

sentences.text: Dia jogging pagi-pagi di pantai setiap hari.
sentences.en: She jogs very early in the morning at the beach every day.

sentences.text: Kami minum kopi pagi-pagi bersama keluarga.
sentences.en: We drink coffee very early in the morning together with family.

note: "Rumah kos" is everyday informal Indonesian for a rented room or boarding house, common among students and workers; also shortened to "kos"; not to be confused with "rumah kontrakan" (a fully rented house).

sentences.text: Saya tinggal di rumah kos dekat kampus.
sentences.en: I live in a boarding house near the campus.

sentences.text: Rumah kos ini murah dan bersih.
sentences.en: This boarding house is cheap and clean.

sentences.text: Dia mencari rumah kos baru bulan ini.
sentences.en: She is looking for a new boarding house this month.

english: this morning (spoken later in the day)
note: "Tadi pagi" means "this morning" when said later in the same day; do not confuse with "pagi ini" which is used closer to the morning itself.

sentences.text: Saya makan nasi tadi pagi.
sentences.en: I ate rice this morning.

sentences.text: Tadi pagi saya pergi ke pasar.
sentences.en: This morning I went to the market.

sentences.text: Dia minum kopi tadi pagi.
sentences.en: He/She drank coffee this morning.

english: this afternoon (spoken later in the day)
note: Used to refer to 'this afternoon' when speaking later in the same day; paired with past events, unlike 'siang ini' which sounds unnatural in speech.

sentences.text: Tadi siang saya makan nasi goreng.
sentences.en: This afternoon I ate fried rice.

sentences.text: Dia pergi ke pasar tadi siang.
sentences.en: She went to the market this afternoon.

sentences.text: Tadi siang cuacanya sangat panas.
sentences.en: This afternoon the weather was very hot.

english: an act of parliament, law(s) of the land
note: Formal/legal term for national laws or acts; more official than 'aturan' (rule) or 'hukum' (law/justice system); often seen in news and civics contexts.

sentences.text: Undang-undang itu melindungi hak semua orang.
sentences.en: That law protects everyone's rights.

sentences.text: Kita harus mengikuti undang-undang di Indonesia.
sentences.en: We must follow the laws in Indonesia.

sentences.text: Guru menjelaskan undang-undang kepada murid.
sentences.en: The teacher explained the law to the students.

english: ..., right? ...have you? ...do you? ...does he/she? ...okay? (seeking confirmation or approval)

note: "Ada yang" means "there are some (that)" or "some (people/things)"; use "ada [noun] yang" when the noun is specified, e.g. "ada teman yang" = "some friends who".

sentences.text: Ada yang mau minum kopi?
sentences.en: Does anyone want to drink coffee?

sentences.text: Ada teman yang datang ke pesta.
sentences.en: Some friends came to the party.

sentences.text: Ada yang suka makan nasi goreng.
sentences.en: Some people like to eat fried rice.

note: "Ahli filsafat" means philosopher; "ahli" means expert/specialist, used with many fields (e.g., ahli kimia = chemist); sometimes shortened to "filsuf" in formal writing.

sentences.text: Dia adalah seorang ahli filsafat terkenal.
sentences.en: He is a famous philosopher.

sentences.text: Ahli filsafat itu suka berpikir mendalam.
sentences.en: That philosopher likes to think deeply.

sentences.text: Saya ingin menjadi ahli filsafat hebat.
sentences.en: I want to become a great philosopher.

note: 'Filsuf' means philosopher; formal/written register, related to 'filsafat' (philosophy); not commonly used in casual speech.

sentences.text: Dia adalah seorang filsuf yang terkenal.
sentences.en: He is a famous philosopher.

sentences.text: Filsuf itu suka bertanya tentang kehidupan.
sentences.en: The philosopher likes to ask about life.

sentences.text: Saya membaca buku tentang seorang filsuf.
